We investigate the preparation of quantum states in cavity magnomechanics using a two-dimensional magnetic material. Specifically, we examine the effect of a magnetic substance with easy-plane anisotropy, represented by a square lattice of Ising spins, coupled to an optical cavity. The spins interact with a standing wave of optical photons, generating an effective magnetic field that parametrically drives the cavity's mechanical resonator. This interaction enables us to analyze the conditions necessary for coherent state generation, as well as the characteristics of higher-order quantum states. Our findings demonstrate that the unique properties of easy-plane anisotropy in two-dimensional magnetic materials can facilitate the preparation of non-classical quantum states in cavity magnomechanics. Additionally, we discuss the relevance of our results to materials with easy-plane anisotropy in the Bernal-Goldstone phase and the weak easy-plane limit. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for exploring quantum-state preparation in magnomechanical systems. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for applying our theoretical concepts to experimental setups using materials such as NiCl$_3$ or CuFeO$_2$. Finally, we outline the possible directions for future research based on our study.

Developing a reliable and maintainable software system is a complex task that current industry methods struggle to achieve. One major obstacle is the difficulty in accurately determining the semantic meaning of the code, which leads to poor decision-making during software development. Abstractions such as control flow graphs and abstract syntax trees have been used to represent code semantically, but they fall short in capturing the program's high-level structure and long-term properties. In contrast, graph neural networks offer a promising approach to encoding code semantically, and our research builds upon this concept by introducing a global representation of the code using graph neural networks. Our method, called GOR, enables the capture of code characteristics at a higher level by considering both local and global features. Through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of GOR in predicting code semantics, outperforming existing methods significantly. Furthermore, we show that GOR can be applied to various graph neural networks and provide insights into its architecture. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the implementation of GOR on PyTorch, as well as the pre-trained models used in our experiments. Our research has far-reaching implications for the development of reliable software systems and graph neural networks. By enabling the global semantic analysis of code, we can develop more accurate models and improve software development decision-making. Federated Learning aims to train a model without collecting user data by allowing clients to contribute their local optimization progress to a central server. A novel approach, Federated Distillation, trains the global model by aggregating gradients on the server and distributing parameter gradients among clients. However, this method has a high communication cost due to exchanging dense gradient tensors. In this paper, we propose an efficient communication strategy for Federated Distillation by introducing a compact representation of gradient information. Specifically, we develop a method to approximate parameter gradients with a small set of representative vectors, reducing communication cost and enabling efficient training on mobile devices. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly decreases communication rounds by 90% and achieves comparable performance with Federated Distillation. It also outperforms existing Federated Learning methods by 2-4% in terms of accuracy. The proposed approach is also resilient to data heterogeneity and allows training a ResNet-18 on ImageNet with clients having as few as 1 image each. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexgu2019/fed_distillation.

In this research, we investigate risk-averse reinforcement learning in dynamic settings with varying reward distributions and time-varying transition probabilities. Our goal is to minimize a fixed quantile function of the cumulative discounted rewards, which measures downside risk. This algorithm adaptively collects data to estimate the Markov decision process and its risk function using a sample-complexity analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the separation between dynamic and static regret in risk-aware reinforcement learning. Finally, we evaluate our approach on a real-world appointment scheduling problem, which shows its effectiveness in managing downside risk. Notably, our algorithm converges to a near-optimal solution even when the risk function is not smooth. This work significantly improves upon existing research in risk-aware reinforcement learning by providing a dynamic regret bound, which is linear in the time horizon, and achieving a dimension-free sample complexity. This research is the first to apply adaptive data collection in reinforcement learning to estimate the risk function. With continued advancements, machine learning is poised to revolutionize the field of high-entropy alloys, enabling rapid and accurate design of novel materials with tailored properties.

The cultural background of video creators significantly influences the content, which can result in a search outcome's cultural and social diversity being underrepresented. This is known as Origin Variety Bias (OVB). For instance, a search query for "music" may yield more videos from Western origin than from Eastern origin. In this paper, we introduce a novel auditing approach to measure OVB in video search outcomes. Our method employs virtual agents with different origins to simulate human search behavior. The effectiveness of graph neural networks heavily relies on high-quality node labels, which are often scarce in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, we employ pseudo-labeling, a popular technique that generates reliable labels through model predictions. However, pseudo-labeling faces a critical issue: the quality of generated labels deteriorates as more pseudo-labels are produced. To address this problem, we present a novel approach called QFlow, which integrates quality estimation and pseudo-labeling into a unified framework. QFlow enhances pseudo-labeling by dynamically adjusting its strategy based on the quality of existing labels, preventing a decline in label quality. Through experiments on four datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of QFlow over state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of QFlow's performance under different parameter configurations. Furthermore, we successfully apply QFlow to three challenging, node-classification tasks. The source code of QFlow is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-wu/QFlow.

In video analysis, aligning frames to a reference template is a common task. Traditional methods using optical flow or feature-based matching can be computationally expensive and prone to inaccuracies when the motion is long or the tracking fails. We introduce PatchNet, a novel, efficient, and robust template alignment technique that uses shallow networks to match super-pixels or image patches instead of individual features. PatchNet significantly outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy, achieving up to 130x faster while retaining a 6% higher AUC score in multi-object tracking. We also demonstrate its success in other video analysis tasks such as vehicle tracking and action recognition, outperforming the state-of-the-art in many cases. The deployment of AI systems is increasingly influenced by opaque, high-stakes decisions made by their developers. There is a pressing need for incident reporting and knowledge sharing to avoid future AI failures. This paper introduces the AI Incident Repository, a public database of real-world AI incidents, and outlines the benefits and potential uses of the repository for advancing AI safety. The repository currently contains 76 documented incidents, spanning topics such as inaccurate image recognition, robotic collisions, and fatal self-driving car accidents. The AI Incident Repository is accessible online and invites contributions with established guidelines for submission and review. By crowdsourcing incident submissions and fostering a collaborative environment within the AI safety community, we can work together to prevent future AI failures.

Structured text recognition aims to identify and extract specific patterns of text from images. The challenge lies in predicting various structured text outputs, such as different date formats, which can lead to multiple possible readings of the same image. Current approaches often rely on sequence-to-sequence models that utilize attention mechanisms to focus on particular image regions, but these models struggle with date recognition due to their limited capacity to generate diverse output sequences. To overcome this shortcoming, we introduce a new training method that favors the use of regular expressions in structured text recognition tasks. The proposed method, called RegFavor, encourages the model to produce sequences compliant with predefined regular expressions, which are learned from labeled data. RegFavor can be applied to any existing structured text recognition model and is particularly beneficial for tasks that involve regular expression patterns, such as date, time, and semantic text matching. We evaluate RegFavor on the widely used ICDAR 2013 CURT challenge and the TextFront dataset for date recognition, achieving significant improvements of 4.7 and 3.1% respectively, in terms of word error rate. The code and models are available on GitHub.

Developing a text-to-SQL model that can learn semantic meaning is extremely challenging, particularly in the absence of database information. This study proposes a novel cross-domain approach, enabling a text-to-SQL model to gain insight from diverse databases, thereby enhancing its semantic understanding. To achieve this, we present the TextSQL Complex dataset, comprising 4,000 complex instances, along with two database schemes. This dataset is designed to evaluate a text-to-SQL model's ability to comprehend database information and generate semantically valid SQL queries. Furthermore, we introduce a cross-domain language model, equipped with an auxiliary table description task, to facilitate semantic learning across different domains. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art models by a significant margin of 10.4% in terms of execution accuracy. Notably, it achieves this improvement while maintaining comparable token-level accuracy with a model lacking this auxiliary task. This research showcases the effectiveness of cross-domain training in text-to-SQL models and highlights the significance of semantic understanding in database query generation. The proposed model and TextSQL Complex dataset are now publicly available.

This research introduces an innovative a posteriori error control strategy for a generalized Boussinesq model, applicable to heated substance processing. The approach simultaneously targets two critical goals: maintaining temperature differences and fluid velocity vector gradients within predetermined limits. A fully implantable error control module is designed to adjust the temporal and spatial error control parameters, ensuring adherence to the specified goal thresholds. A post-processing technique is also developed to effectively determine the error estimates required for the error control module. This method is successfully demonstrated in a heated substance processing scenario, with the goal of preventing hotspots in the temperature field and excessive shear in the velocity vector field. The error control module is capable of adjusting the time step and spatial refinement until the goal thresholds are met, as shown in the numerical experiments. Furthermore, the error estimates are validated to be consistent across different spatial discretization methods. This study showcases the efficacy of the proposed error control strategy in a real-world heated substance processing application. The research also highlights the potential for the error control strategy to be adapted for other Boussinesq model configurations and diverse industrial applications. In a game of limited confidence, players compete to make accurate predictions on a continuous scale, but only with incomplete information about their opponents' abilities. Each player sets an initial "opinion" level and then chooses a "structural equilibrium" strategy that balances taking risks and staying within bounds. The game's unique dynamics are a complex interplay of these two components, which evolve separately yet connected. The opinion level becomes a public variable that influences the structural equilibrium, while also being updated based on the difference between the player's guess and the actual outcome. We show that in a 2-player game with a bounded risk parameter, both the opinion and structural equilibrium converge to a unique state of equilibrium, which we calculate and find that it depends on the risk level. Furthermore, we explore the scenario with unbounded risk and discover that the system can converge to multiple equilibriums through numerical analysis. Transcription is the initial step of gene expression, and its efficiency and speed significantly impact cellular behavior. Although transcription is a critical process, there's a notable lack of comprehensive tools to study it on a genome-wide scale. To address this, we've developed a novel method combining high-resolution sequencing data with chromatin structure information to analyze transcription across entire genomes. This method allows for the identification of transcription start sites, activity levels, and directionality in various cellular conditions. We've applied this method to human cells to investigate transcription and demonstrate its efficacy by uncovering previously unknown patterns, including widespread RNA production delays. This method is now available for public use.

When subjected to high shear rates, many colloidal suspensions undergo a sudden thickening, characterized by a drastic increase in viscosity. This shear thickening phenomenon is commonly observed in various particle suspensions and can lead to the development of unusual and complex behaviors. Despite its prevalence, the underlying physics of shear thickening remains poorly understood, particularly in global suspension dynamics and structure formation. In this study, researchers have identified a universal scaling relationship between the shear rate and volume fraction of particles, which explains the shear thickening process in many colloidal suspensions. By developing a simplified theoretical model based on shear thickening mechanics, the researchers derived this scaling relationship and validated it with various particle suspensions, including Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. This scaling relationship provides a general framework for predicting the shear thickening behavior of different particle suspensions and their transition to fluid-like flow. Furthermore, the researchers found that their theoretical model can also explain the formation of particle clusters and the development of shear stress softening, which are complex phenomena observed in many colloidal suspensions. This study sheds new light on the shear thickening phenomenon and its associated complex behaviors, providing a general understanding of the shear thickening process in particle suspensions. Additionally, the researchers suggest that their findings can be applied to other shear thickening systems, including polymers and foams. Overall, this study significantly advances our understanding of shear thickening and its associated complex behaviors, paving the way for future research in this field.

The Web is the largest knowledge repository in existence, yet its responsiveness to user queries is hindered by personalization filters that distort the scope of visible information. This study examines the extent to which Google's Web search personalization biases the results of computational methods designed to assess a topic's presence on the Web. Our findings reveal that the influence of personalization filters can lead these computational methods to underestimate the Web's pertinent information by as much as 75%. This research highlights the limitations of relying solely on computational methods for evaluating a topic's presence on the Web and the importance of incorporating human input to validate these estimates. Moreover, our study provides empirical evidence of the significant impact of personalization biases on the Web search results, which could potentially be exploited to manipulate public opinion and informants' opinions through selective information promotion or suppression. This research has implications for the development of more accurate computational methods and the role of human judgment in evaluating a topic's presence on the Web. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between search engine algorithms, human perception, and the dissemination of information. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been highly effective in image
recognition, but can also be applied to a directed graph recognition task.
We have adapted CNNs to suit graph representation and utilized them to generate
program models from flow diagrams, achieving a 90% accuracy rate in graph
reconstruction. Our approach, known as GRCNN, comprises an input pre-processing
stage that converts flow diagrams into a suitable format, followed by a CNN
layer that extracts key path patterns. A fully connected layer then determines
the program's control flow structure. Our experiments demonstrate the superior
performance of GRCNN over existing state-of-the-art methods. The project,
including code and datasets, is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang/GRCNN.

In climate research, diminution techniques are employed to remove non-perturbative components from statistical models, often using approximations like Taylor expansions. This paper provides a clear definition of diminution techniques and examines their implications on stability and bifurcation analysis in climate dynamics. A concise review of dimension reduction methods is included for context. Several examples illustrate the application of diminution techniques in climate dynamics, highlighting their potential to streamline model computations and reveal novel insights. This document aims to serve as a concise reference for researchers transitioning from dynamical systems to climate dynamics. Due to space constraints, some discussions are kept brief and central results are summarized. Further details can be found in the referenced articles and books.

Compositional data analysis is a technique primarily used to investigate the relationships between compositional data objects. It has significant applications across various scientific fields, including environmental science, biology, and medicine. This chapter provides an introduction to compositional data analysis by defining essential concepts and outlining the necessary linear algebra mathematics. It also explores visualization methods and the interpretation of results, which are essential skills for researchers to master. A step-by-step example is used to demonstrate compositional data analysis procedures. This chapter serves as a reference for the subsequent chapters in this book, which delve into more advanced compositional data analysis methods. A comprehensive R package called AICcpo is utilized to facilitate the compositional data analysis procedures discussed in this chapter. Time-series forecasting has been expanded into storytelling by generating narratives that include future time-series data. However, current models are limited by their requirement to be specialized in specific domains, which hinders their applicability to new domains. To overcome this, we present TCube, a neural story generation model that can adapt to various domains without being tailored to those domains. TCube achieves this through the use of a time-series embedding module that automatically extracts key time-series characteristics and a set of domain-agnostic story templates that facilitate narrative generation. Experimental results demonstrate TCube's ability to outperform existing models in both domain-specific and domain-unknown settings. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of TCube's performance. The source code for TCube is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyinliu/TCube.

Developers often encounter online resources that aid their problem-solving when encountering bugs or challenges while coding. On Stack Overflow, external links are shared by developers to seek solutions, and these links can be categorized into useful and spam-related content. This study aims to categorize these links into Stack Overflow questions to determine their purpose and whether they are relevant to the original problems discussed. A proposed framework involves classifying links into useful or spam-based on specific criteria and then evaluating their relevance to the original questions. A 10-member panel successfully categorized 1,000 links using this framework with 92% accuracy, and further analysis revealed that Stack Overflow moderators play a crucial role in maintaining the platform's link quality through deletion processes. Our findings suggest that link quality on Stack Overflow is primarily affected by spam, and improvements can be made by enhancing moderators' tools to distinguish between useful and relevant links to the original questions. Ultimately, implementing these changes can boost users' trust in the platform and promote a better browsing experience. To effectively address climate change, it's crucial to engage the public through climate information. However, current climate research data is inaccessible to the general public due to its complex and technical nature, presented mainly through academic publications and specialized repositories. This project proposes a climate data repository that enables researchers to document their findings in a way that fosters public understanding. We also present a method for indexing and disseminating climate research in an accessible manner. We conducted a study to evaluate the impact of our approach by comparing the outcomes of two workshops, one that provided climate researchers with data from our repository and one without. The results show that workshops with our repository lead to more innovative policy recommendations and a higher level of participant knowledge.

To facilitate the development of AI-assisted medicine, we've introduced a domain generalization approach for extracting symptom and disease events from unstructured medical records. Our method focuses on leaving out source domain data during training and demonstrates superior performance on a real-world dataset, outperforming the best feature-based approach by 10.6% in terms of F1-score and 4.4% in terms of F1-score in a leave-one-domain-out setting. Our method's effectiveness stems from its ability to create diverse training data and prevent overfitting. Furthermore, we've observed that using pre-trained BERT representations of medical entities enhances our method's overall accuracy. Our method and data are available for public use at https://github.com/linzhi2002/Generalize-EE.

This study investigates the estimation of nonlinear eigenfunctions in a dependent context. We introduce a direct method of estimating eigenfunctions based on a minimization of rational interpolation, which has lower computational requirements than existing approaches. Under specific conditions, this method yields adaptive estimation of eigenfunctions with optimal rate of convergence. We also demonstrate that this estimator is robust to model misspecification and achieve a convergence rate of $n^{-\frac{2s+1}{4s+3}}$, where $s$ is the smoothness of eigenfunctions. We further extend this approach to the estimation of nonlinear diffusion processes and the analysis of principal curves in a dependent context. Our results are supported by both theoretical and simulation-based evidence. 

\textbf{Keywords:} Adaptive estimation, nonlinear eigenfunctions, minimization of rational interpolation, dependent data, principal curves.

This paper introduces a new method for compressive representation of data streams in terms of independent components, utilizing a limited number of measurements. It presents theoretical arguments for the accuracy of this representation and proposes multiple algorithms for achieving it. One proposed method is a compressive ICA algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, and another is a robust online algorithm for the Oja problem that outperforms existing methods. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in achieving high-quality representations using significantly fewer sensors than traditional approaches. Additionally, the paper explores the application of this method to the recovery of hidden sources from mixtures of compressive measurements, and its implementation in the SPARTA MATLAB toolbox is detailed. Key findings indicate that our approach can achieve better performance than previous methods under certain conditions. Furthermore, the paper discovers that a specific variant of the CICA method is analogous to the Kaczmarz algorithm when applied to orthogonal vectors, and that another variant is an online extension of the JADE algorithm. Finally, the paper presents a new gradient descent method for the Oja problem and the CICA objective function, and observes that this method is robust to errors in the Hessian matrix. All source code is publicly available through the SPARTA MATLAB toolbox.

The effectiveness of programmable phase discs in correcting aberrations in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) is explored through simulation-based analysis. By modeling the phase disc as a thin crystal that introduces a crystalline phase into electron beams, we demonstrate that it can correct the defocusing and spherical aberrations affecting TEM imaging. Our simulations reveal that a phase disc with a thickness of 10 nanometers can provide up to 90% correction for both types of aberrations, operating within a focus range of -10 to 10 micrometers. Notably, the phase disc's imaging performance surpasses that of a 10-micrometer-thin physical aperture. However, our model also shows that the phase disc's transmission efficiency declines by approximately 20% due to phase disc-induced beam diffraction. This beam diffraction is found to be the primary factor limiting the phase disc's ability to correct higher-order aberrations. Ultimately, our study indicates that a phase disc with a higher refractive index or thinner thickness could enhance its aberration-correcting capabilities. Additionally, integrating multiple phase discs could potentially correct higher-order aberrations and provide improved imaging outcomes. This paper examines how to evaluate expressions containing floating-point operations with uncertain results. We develop a method to reliably determine the precision of those expressions. This approach uses a graph theory framework to represent the uncertainty propagation model. We show that this model can solve a broad class of assessment problems, which we call Problem 1, and identify a specific instance of this problem, known as Problem 2, that can be solved efficiently. Climate change conspiracy theories thrive online, with false claims spreading rapidly across social media platforms. This paper investigates the spread of one such theory, asserting carbon dioxide has a negligible impact on the climate, on Twitter and Facebook. We gathered and analyzed a substantial dataset of 11 months, comprising 1.8 million tweets and 38,000 Facebook posts. Our analysis reveals the social media footprint of this conspiracy leaves users uninformed about scientific evidence. We identified the conspiracy's dissemination to be seasonal, peaking during US election periods and coinciding with a decline in user engagement on Twitter. Our results also show that Facebook appears to be a more favorable platform for this conspiracy theory, with higher engagement rates compared to Twitter. We observed the conspiracy's proponents primarily use unverified accounts to spread the theory. Notably, our analysis suggests climate change conspiracy theories may not be a primary concern on social media, with their spread being relatively limited compared to other topics. We advocate for social media companies to take proactive measures in reducing the visibility of such conspiracy theories. Our dataset is available for research purposes at https://climateconspiracy.github.io/.

This research introduces a novel, partitioning model for images, where each segment of the partitioning undergoes separate optimization to minimize its total variation. This paper investigates the effect of framework exploration in unverified assertions within SMT solvers. Unverified assertions in interactive proof assistants serve as a framework for guiding search within SMT solvers. By categorizing model variables, unverified assertions direct the SMT solver to explore relevant cases, enhancing its efficiency. However, the current method of asserting variables does not account for the framework in which they reside. As a result, the SMT solver may waste time examining unrelated variables or ignore pivotal ones within the framework. To address this limitation, we introduce two new assertions: "exploring-in" and "exploring-out," which enable the SMT solver to focus on variables within the selected framework. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating these assertions significantly boosts the SMT solver's performance in generating interactive proofs. Furthermore, we present a strategy for automatically generating "exploring-in" assertions, thus streamlining the process of creating interactive proofs. Lastly, we showcase the incorporation of these assertions in a verified framework for generating interactive proofs within the Coq proof assistant. This verified framework, along with the SMT solver and Coq code, are available for public use.

The parquet theory is a modern approach to describe strongly-correlated electronic systems, particularly those exhibiting density wave and flux phase behaviors. Traditionally, it has been presented as a set of integral equations derived from a cumulant expansion of the two-particle interaction within a Fermi sea background. This work reinterprets parquet theory as a Hamiltonian-based framework rooted in a perturbative expansion of the system's Hamiltonian with respect to a certain 'deviation' interaction. This 'deviation' interaction is shown to be equivalent to the cumulant expansion's 'correction' interaction, and is demonstrated to capture the effects of higher-order cumulant terms. By establishing parquet theory within this framework, we can reexamine its underlying assumptions and provide new insights into its structure and content. This reformulation also facilitates the integration of parquet theory with other related approaches, such as the cluster or Luttinger liquid expansions. As a concrete example, we derive a parquet theory description for the half-filled Hubbard model, and show that it can be integrated with the cluster expansion. This integration allows us to obtain a more comprehensive description of the system, and to identify key features of its phase diagram. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this reformulated parquet theory to other problems in strongly-correlated systems.

In a nematic superconductor with triplet Cooper pairs, we investigate how applying a magnetic field orientated perpendicular to the plane influences the superconducting properties. Above a certain field threshold, the superconducting gap exhibits a paramagnetic increase due to the alignment of paired electrons. We derive the self-consistent equations governing this behavior in a model doped smecto-chiral superconductor and demonstrate that its transition to the normal state can be either first or second order. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of this paramagnetic effect on the superconductor's topological properties. Interestingly, the paired electrons' magnetic response remains quantized, yet the superconductor's topological characteristics can change continuously. Lastly, we discuss how this paramagnetic effect might be observed in experiments on materials like $\rm{Cu_ {1.53}Ir_ {0.47}Se_3$ and $\rm{CeCoIn_5$.}\$

We introduce a new learning paradigm called Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL), which is a game-theoretic approach that synergizes online learning and offline model selection. In MEL, the learner aims to minimize the worst-case regret compared to the optimal model, while the adversary seeks to maximize the regret relative to the optimal solution. Our key findings include the development of a general MEL algorithm, which achieves a sublinear regret bound, as well as a variant of the algorithm that yields linear regret in the strong regret setting. Furthermore, we demonstrate the optimality of the MEL approach by showing that its regret bound is asymptotically optimal. MEL offers flexibility, as it can accommodate a range of model selection methods and adversaries, allowing it to outperform existing online learning algorithms in several scenarios. Our experiments verify the efficacy of MEL. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyinliu/MEL.

This research assesses the evolution of data complexity in modern Western music by analyzing the lyrics and song titles from top 10 hit songs in the US from 1964 to 2019. A novel estimator, the Standardized Enhanced Inference Function, is proposed as a reliable treatment of potential outcomes in the presence of high-dimensional data. It integrates the predictive power of machine learning models with the influence of key variables, estimated using a high-dimensional model, to calculate counterfactuals. The SEIF estimator is a combination of the Standardized Inverse Probability Weighting method and an efficient estimator, achieving asymptotic efficiency with a finite number of simulations. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and an application to a real-world data set. The R code used in this research is available on GitHub.

This paper presents a novel concept of robust offline reinforcement learning under data manipulation, proposing the first fraud-resilient offline RL framework. It assumes a data curator provides a reliable subset of transition data while an adversary may include fraudulent data. This data curator is assumed to have knowledge of the reward function but the adversary has no information about it. This results in a policy iteration algorithm that incorporates a new value estimation objective. Furthermore, we theoretically prove its convergence and provide empirical evidence of its effectiveness. To achieve this, we employ the logarithmic convexity method, deriving a controlability criterion based on the logarithmic convexity of a related non-smooth function. The result shows that the system can be controlled precisely within a finite time frame using instantaneous controls, assuming the logarithmic convexity condition is satisfied. A model representing the temperature distribution in a thin rod satisfies this condition, thereby confirming the precise controllability of the system in this specific case. However, the condition is not satisfied for the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to the conclusion that the system may not be controllable using only instantaneous controls in this scenario. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the approximate controllability of the system can be achieved using a control with a small time delay, confirming that the system can be approximated closely within a finite time frame using a control with a small time delay. This paper examines the diverse categories of out-of-domain text and how they are recognized. A dataset with 6,000 labeled sentences, spanning 10 categories of out-of-domain text, is introduced and made available. Models such as transformer-based classification and transformer-based chatbot, initially designed for in-domain text, are assessed on this dataset. Our analysis reveals that certain models can effectively identify specific types of out-of-domain text across various categories, while others struggle with most types of out-of-domain text. Additionally, we investigate the impact of training data quantity on out-of-domain text recognition and find that increasing the training data from 1k to 10k improves performance across all categories. However, further data augmentation yields diminishing returns beyond 10k. Our dataset and code are accessible for replication of our results. A chatbot prototype that recognizes out-of-domain text is also demonstrated. Its source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/aleksandr-vladimirov/ood-detector. Our analysis utilizes the APOLLO retrieval code to examine the available near-infrared data from GJ 229B, aiming to shed light on its atmospheric properties. We employed a range of atmospheric models, including those with and without cloud formations, as well as models that considered various chemical species and chemical reactions. Our results indicate that GJ 229B's atmosphere likely contains a substantial amount of methane, ammonia, and water, with clouds also being a plausible feature. We also found that our best-fit models are characterized by high pressures, with cloud formations being more suitable when using the GJ 229B spectrum in combination with its mass and evolutionary history. Furthermore, our study suggests that GJ 229B's atmosphere may be experiencing chemical changes due to its low luminosity, with the resulting formation of phosphine and other metal hydrides being unlikely. Our study's findings are consistent with the possibility of GJ 229B having a substellar mass, with further observations needed to confirm our results and provide more insights into this enigmatic object. In software testing, instructors often struggle to assess students' test planning skills, which are crucial for effective testing. To address this challenge, we developed and tested two evaluation methods that utilize student-created test plans: (1) inquiry-based conceptual feedback and (2) detailed graded feedback with evaluation criteria and ratings. The inquiry-based method involves providing students with general feedback related to test planning, whereas the detailed graded feedback method entails evaluating students' test plans against specific criteria and providing numerical ratings. Through an empirical study of 120 students in two university courses, we found that inquiry-based conceptual feedback led to higher student satisfaction, improved perceived quality of teaching, and greater effort to improve their test plans, compared to detailed graded feedback. However, both methods showed comparable improvements in student learning. Based on our findings, we recommend using inquiry-based conceptual feedback as a more effective and efficient evaluation method for assessing students' test planning skills. The study's results can be applied to other areas of software testing education, and the inquiry-based approach can be adapted to other subjects as well. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been widely adopted across various tasks due to their effectiveness in learning node representations from graph data. Our findings also show that GCNs with adaptive graph filtering methods outperform their non-adaptive counterparts in various graph machine learning tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a novel adaptive graph filtering method that surpasses the performance of existing methods and provide a theoretical justification for its effectiveness. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

We have developed two entropy estimation protocols based on quantum principles. The first, a non-linear approach, uses a von Neumann entropy probe and achieves an accuracy of $\varepsilon$ with a sample size of $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})$. Both protocols are subject to the constraint of minimal entropy per quantum state. The linear approach is particularly efficient when entropy is high. The protocols' performance is validated through numerical experiments on random quantum systems. The developed methods are expected to be valuable in quantum dynamics analysis and research into quantum many-body systems. Shadows play a crucial role in rendering realistic images and have numerous applications in computer vision. However, solving inverse problems in shadows can be extremely challenging due to the lack of a proper shadow formulation in differentiable rendering pipelines. To address this limitation, we present an innovative, flexible, and efficient shadow evaluation algorithm that is fully differentiable and can be used in various rendering engines. Our approach is founded on an effective shadow area formulation that considers surface orientation, light source position, and pixel position. To accelerate shadow evaluation, we also developed a k-d tree acceleration method, which significantly enhances the shadow engine's performance. As a result, this framework enables the development of shadow-related loss functions, making it possible to train neural networks differentiable shadow evaluation. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we successfully applied it to two inverse problems: estimating 3D shapes from silhouettes and recovering scene parameters from shadowcast. Our experiments show that our framework outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuzheng/DeepShadow.

This paper introduces a novel probabilistic framework for modeling origin-destination demand on an urban network. The framework is based on an independent and identically distributed assumption, which is validated using statistical methods from a daily traffic demand matrix in Beijing, China. The results show that the distribution of link flows deviates from normality, but the origin-destination demand matrix exhibits elliptical symmetry. This finding enables the application of a Mahalanobis distance metric in clustering analysis, which outperforms the traditional Euclidean metric in identifying distinct patterns of daily demand. Furthermore, the framework's ability to model demand distributions is demonstrated by calculating the cumulative probability distributions of zone-to-zone link flows and their cumulative sums. The ultimate goal is to utilize this framework in real-time feedback control systems to inform decision-making. The integration of this framework and real-time feedback control systems holds significant potential for the optimization of daily traffic management in urban areas. To assess the ability of lifelong reinforcement learning to retain knowledge across multiple tasks, we developed a continuous evaluation framework called L2Explorer. This environment presents agents with a sequence of tasks that demand different navigation skills in a map, characterized by various sizes. Underlying each task is a state-space function and a reward mechanism that remains consistent across all maps, whereas the target location and reward structure change from one task to another. Our evaluation indicates that models which effectively preserve knowledge and adapt it across tasks outperform those focused solely on short-term learning. In this research, we explore the effectiveness of combining multiple input modalities for retinal image analysis. We focus on classifying glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy (DR) using optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus image features. Our results indicate that integrating OCT and fundus features enhances the performance of OCT alone. We also found that a simple fusion of these modalities outperforms more complex multiview deep learning networks. Intention exploration in goal-oriented dialogue involves navigating various conversational goals to gather data for a self-initiating dialogue system. Current methods are limited by their reliance on goal achievement, which can lead to data inefficiency and biased language learning. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new approach that utilizes pre-trained language models to directly learn spoken language, and incorporates a contrastive loss to enhance intention exploration. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in producing more diverse and effective responses compared to existing benchmarks. The source code and data are available on GitHub for reproducibility.

A significant challenge in this task is the presence of incorrect positive instances, which are difficult to address through traditional accuracy metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art models on the Minippo and VQA-CE datasets, which focus on evaluating this issue. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the method's effectiveness. The proposed approach is now available on our GitHub repository.

The development of social relationship graphs has become increasingly significant in various fields. Although deep learning methods have been successfully applied to graph creation, they often rely on pre-trained nodes and edges. This paper presents a new, self-contained graph creation network that produces social relationship graphs without requiring pre-trained nodes or edges. Our model is specifically designed for social relationship graphs but can be adapted for other graph creation tasks with minor modifications. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms existing graph creation models. The source code for this paper can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang4/GraphCreation.

Deep neural networks excel at image recognition, but their ability to process graph-structured data is limited. We introduce the Active Graph Message Transfer Network (AGMTN), a model that efficiently handles graph-structured data for visual recognition tasks. By integrating graph convolutional layers with a self-attention mechanism, AGMTN can effectively process node and edge features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AGMTN in node, edge, and triplets recognition, achieving superior performance on the ScanNet dataset. Additionally, our model provides a versatile framework for other graph-based vision tasks. We also introduce the SemGraph dataset, a benchmark for semantic graph recognition. High-resolution hyperspectral images possess sufficient spectral and spatial details to facilitate semantic segmentation. Nevertheless, current deep learning methods are often hindered by limited training datasets. To overcome this challenge, we propose an innovative framework that integrates HR hyperspectral images into standard RGB images, thereby enhancing segmentation performance. The framework comprises two primary components: a) a spectral fusion module that incorporates spectral information into an RGB image using an optimal band selection strategy; b) a weakly-guided training approach that utilizes the HR hyperspectral image as a weak label to supplement limited semantic segmentation datasets. The framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated through semantic segmentation experiments on various hyperspectral images, which yielded superior results compared to conventional methods. To facilitate efficient shopping, session-based product suggestion generates a list of items based on user behavior within a single shopping session. Most current methods focus on modeling user behavior over time, but ignore the interdependencies between suggestions. To address this, we propose a self-training framework that leverages both user queries and previously suggested items. We achieve this through a two-stage co-training approach, combining the session encoder with a guided self-learning module. The session encoder captures temporal user behavior and generates initial suggestion labels, while the self-learning module refines these labels by incorporating the encoded information of previously suggested items. We conduct experiments on a real-world e-commerce dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method over existing session-based recommendation techniques. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaozh/SSGCR.

Social media platforms are increasingly being used to disseminate misogynistic content, which is considered a severe form of online harassment. The widespread nature of Arabic misogynistic content on social media makes it challenging to detect and address. Current approaches for identifying misogynistic content are limited to English and focus on detection only. In response, we introduce a novel framework for translingual misogynistic content detection and encompasses three sub-tasks: detection, offense minimization, and toxicity classification. We also propose a new dataset consisting of 4,800 annotated tweets in both Arabic and English. Our framework achieves superior performance compared to baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-task learning and pre-trained language models in addressing these sub-tasks. The proposed framework and dataset will facilitate future research into misogynistic content mitigation. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AlaaTawel/Misogyny-ARABERT.

This research introduces a novel configuration-dependent security framework for mobile robotic arms, combining Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Invariant Constraints to effectively safeguard the system against adverse inputs. The security framework is integrated with a predictive routine, addressing limitations by allowing for secure path planning. The integrated method is demonstrated through simulation, which highlights its capability to ensure secure movement along a desired path for a mobile robotic arm. Furthermore, this research is extended to an actual mobile manipulator robot, the Turtlebot, with successful outcomes shown in simulation. The presented approach offers a practical solution for high-stakes applications, such as search and rescue operations. This research introduces a text summarization approach centered on graph theory, focusing on an extractive methodology that identifies key sentences to comprise a summary. Two core components are developed: a sentence similarity assessment module and a summary module. The former employs a graph-based framework to determine similarity between sentences, incorporating multiple semantic elements, whereas the latter employs a greedy search algorithm to generate the summary. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology in producing summaries that equal those of leading extractive text summarization algorithms in terms of accuracy. Moreover, this approach is adaptable to various other graph-based extractive algorithms, making it a versatile framework for text summarization. The source code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/lethu2709/Text-Summarization. Additionally, pre-generated summarization graphs and hyperparameters are available at https://github.com/lethu2709/Text-Sum Hyperparameters. Evaluation metrics and summary examples can be found at https://github.com/lethu2709/Text-Summary-Examples. This paper was presented at the 2021 International Conference on Big Data, Data Mining and Knowledge Engineering.

Natural language understanding in reinforcement learning has been limited by traditional, representation-based approaches. These methods treat words as isolated symbols, ignoring their semantic connections. In contrast, recent developments in reinforcement learning have led to the creation of more authentic language models. This overview will examine various tasks within the realm of natural language reinforcement learning, focusing on instances where prior work has employed artificial language representations. It will detail the benefits of incorporating semantic relationships between words within state descriptions. Additionally, this overview will introduce the MELTING dataset, which was designed to facilitate the development of more legitimate language representations through reinforcement learning. The MELTING dataset presents a challenging task of forming a coalition of workers by creating appealing job offers, where the state description is comprised of words with inherent semantic connections. The overview will also present a baseline comparison of the performance of authentic versus isolated word representations in this dataset. Furthermore, this overview will outline potential avenues for future research within the natural language reinforcement learning domain. These opportunities include the incorporation of illegitimate word relationships, multi-modal state descriptions, and more. By pushing the boundaries of natural language reinforcement learning, we can develop more authentic models that better reflect the underlying semantic connections between words. This, in turn, can lead to the creation of more effective state representations that facilitate the resolution of complex problems within this domain. The accuracy of automated essay grading depends heavily on how well it's been trained, but improving a model requires a vast amount of annotated data, which can be expensive to obtain. This paper explores the effectiveness of data enhancement techniques that improve the quality of training data without requiring additional annotations. We experiment with various methods, including the Transformer architecture, and find that using BERT to generate synthetic samples significantly boosts the model's performance in identifying grammatical errors. This improvement is particularly evident in the model's ability to learn complex, long-range grammatical dependencies. We also found that using synthetic samples can help the model generalize better to new data. Overall, our results show that data enhancement techniques can be an efficient alternative to expanding a model's training dataset with annotated data. This research contributes to the development of more robust automated essay grading models. We have made our code and dataset available for public use.

We present an improved RingCT protocol with accelerated transaction processing times. The original RingCT protocol, integrated into Dash, uses a mixing process to conceal transaction values, but this method significantly increases transaction verification time on the blockchain, limiting processing capacity. Our modified RingCT protocol reduces verification time, making it compatible with the existing protocol for seamless integration into Dash-like cryptocurrencies. The new protocol employs a verifiable mixing process utilizing random number generators and hash functions, resulting in a substantial decrease in verification complexity. The fastest implementation of the original RingCT protocol processes a transaction every 0.9 seconds, while our modified protocol achieves transaction processing rates of 1.5, 2.5, and 3.5 transactions per second, respectively, across three different hardware configurations. The modified RingCT protocol effectively increases the scalability of blockchain-based systems, enabling the processing of a higher transaction volume. The technical details of our modified RingCT protocol are explained in detail, along with an analysis of its security properties. This research presents a novel approach to neural speech synthesis without requiring linguistic annotations. Instead, we employ auditory images extracted directly from raw speech signals as input labels for a synthesis model. We develop a two-part system to generate these auditory images: the first generates melodic structures, and the second transcribes them into text. We then fine-tune a neural synthesis model using this unorthodox text transcription, outperforming a baseline that relies on traditional transcription methods. Notably, our results show that the quality of the synthesized speech improves as the number of extracted auditory images increases. We also conduct a subjective listening test and find that the quality of speech synthesized using our method surpasses that of the baseline. Moreover, we discover that the speech synthesized using our method is more similar to the original speech in terms of prosody. We believe that this approach offers a promising means of bypassing linguistic labels in neural speech synthesis systems. In clinical trials known as basket trials, subsets of patients with specific genetic mutations are treated with a therapy, and its effectiveness is evaluated in patients with the same mutation. A statistical method is developed to estimate the sample size required for each mutation subgroup in basket trials, allowing data sharing between subgroups. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to determine treatment effects in each subgroup, and then calculates the necessary sample size for each mutation subtype. Simulation data are used to validate the new method and compare it to a frequentist approach. Results show that the Bayesian method can accurately estimate the required sample size, and sharing data between subgroups does not negatively impact precision. Conversely, the frequentist method tends to overestimate the necessary sample size when data are shared. This new method is useful for basket trials with limited patient populations and few subgroups. Its code is available on GitHub. Keywords: basket trials, sample size determination, Bayesian, frequentist, non-informative priors, subgroups, sharing data.

Sequential action prediction poses a difficult forecasting challenge due to the inherent unpredictability of future human actions. Current methods using Markov Decision Processes have limitations, as they assume the ability to make decisions based on a complete state description and a fixed decision-making process. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a new approach, Feature Mapping RNN, which combines a radial basis function kernel to transform the state space and a RNN to model the action sequence. This model can learn the representation of state-action information and predict future actions with the optimized representation. Experimental results show significant improvements over existing methods on benchmarks such as the MiniGrid platform and the Charades dataset. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuliu/fmrnn.

A spectacular stellar explosion known as a Great Eruption occurred on April 12, 1985, in the star AD Leo, emitting a massive energy burst that was visible to the naked eye. This explosion significantly reduced the star's brightness, and our study involves analyzing near-Ultraviolet spectra obtained just two days after the explosion to understand the event's impact. The spectra we collected exhibit a unique and complex pattern characterized by broad absorption features, and we employed two different approaches to model these observations. Firstly, we used a hydrodynamic simulation of the explosion's interaction with the star's atmosphere, and secondly, we applied a semi-analytical model to describe the gas dynamics. Both models were then combined with a radiative transfer code to synthesize the spectra. Our models successfully reproduce the observed features, and we identified key similarities between the two approaches, indicating that the explosion's effects are confined to the star's outer layers. Our study also highlights the importance of considering the star's rapid rotation and gas dynamics in the atmosphere to accurately explain the observed spectral patterns. Furthermore, we found that our models are consistent with the star's observed brightness reduction and orbital period, and we speculate that the explosion may have caused the star's spin to accelerate. Our research provides new insights into the physics of Great Eruptions and their effects on rapidly rotating stars, and we suggest that future observations of the star's polar brightness could reveal evidence of its rapid rotation. Additionally, we propose that the star may have undergone a transformation into a R Coronae Borealis variable following the explosion. Our study also highlights the potential of future space-based telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope to observe similar events in other stars. Finally, we note that our research may have implications for understanding the origins of supernovae Type Ia and the evolution of close binary systems. The proposed model is evaluated on three datasets, yielding significant improvements in performance over existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper presents a novel proof that identifies whole number solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, analogous to the Pelage's theorem which states that $a^2+ab+b^2$ must equal a perfect square. The paper further extends Pelage's theorem by generalizing the equation to $a^2+ab+b^2=z^n$. To address this, we introduce a new framework that generates imitation learning algorithms capable of cross-task and cross-domain expertise. These algorithms can learn from static images or videos of expert actions and apply the skills to observe the same class of tasks in other domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two challenging scenarios: navigation in 2D grid worlds and locomotion in 3D environments. Our method outperforms previous work by a significant margin in all cases. Notably, it achieves nearly 100% success rates in some scenarios that other approaches failed on. The code and video are available online at https://github.com/chenxi-yu/CAIO.

This study presents a thorough examination of a versatile authentication system that integrates audio, visual, and thermal modalities. Each modality is examined in isolation and together as a combination, with recognition performance being assessed across diverse environments, distinct devices, and identification/sverification modes. Our investigation utilized the OuluCM dataset, comprising voice, face, and skin surface temperature features, obtained under various conditions. A deep learning approach was applied to extract and represent features from the audio-visual-thermal triplet, which was then subjected to a range of classification techniques. Our analysis reveals that the visual and thermal modalities offer more distinctive characteristics for personal recognition compared to voice, with the combination of these modalities delivering superior performance. Additionally, our findings highlight the challenges posed by device changes and the uniqueness of our approach in combining multiple modalities for authentication. This research is expected to contribute to the development of more robust and versatile individual authentication systems. The code and dataset used in this study are available for public access at https://github.com/ahmed-omar/AVTAuth.

The presence of stellar "threads" within the Milky Way is supported by multiple studies, yet the concept remains debated due to limited observational evidence. We conducted a thorough examination of 1,234,655 stars from the Gaia Data Release 2, searching for the characteristic spatial patterns of these threads. Our analysis revealed that the distribution of stars in the celestial plane does not significantly differ between "thread" stars and the general population. We also found that the radial density of "thread" stars does not exceed that of the overall population. Furthermore, the motion of "thread" stars does not exhibit the expected alignment expected of these threads. The presence of "thread" stars in the Southern Hemisphere, where the Milky Way's plane is observed at its highest elevation, is inconsistent with the expected density of these threads. Our findings suggest that the "threads" are an overinterpreted feature of the Milky Way, and the characteristics of "thread" stars can be replicated by randomly selected stars. We propose that the classification of "thread" stars should be revised based on more stringent criteria to ensure the accuracy of these stars' spatial and motion data. Ultimately, the "threads" should be reevaluated in light of new data, and their existence should be confirmed through more conclusive evidence before being incorporated into the model of the Milky Way's structure. The goal of Visual Item Transfer, a sub-field of Visual Fashion Design, is to create digital images of clothing and accessories by modifying existing items. To achieve this, we propose a new approach called VICTOR, a neural network that detects discrepancies in images by comparing the expected outcome with actual modifications. VICTOR's architecture is based on a self-attention mechanism and is specifically designed for fashion applications. We also introduce a new dataset called FashionVQ, which was created by combining existing fashion datasets to provide a wide range of reference images with semantic segmentations. FashionVQ was used to train a contrastive model that enhances the performance of VICTOR. Our experiments show that VICTOR outperforms other visual similarity-based methods and serves as a crucial component of the visual pipeline. Additionally, VICTOR's capabilities extend beyond fashion design to other visual editing tasks. Our code and dataset are available for public use.

Federated Learning can be vulnerable to data heterogeneity and slow convergence, but introducing local data accumulation has improved its resilience. Nonetheless, conventional synchronization of local averages may still be hindered by extreme data variations, leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose FedBuffBA, a novel FL protocol that enables asynchronous accumulation and accommodates disparate data distributions without constraining user gradients. FedBuffBA combines buffered gradient smoothing and decaying learning rates to create a more robust and efficient framework, and our experimental results demonstrate its superior convergence capabilities compared to state-of-the-art FL methods. Additionally, we provide a convergence analysis for FedBuffBA and show its theoretical guarantees for achieving stationarity and making progress towards the optimal solution. Our findings align with the empirical evidence presented. FedBuffBA is now available as an open-source implementation.

Temporal changes in marine environments can significantly impact autonomous robot navigation, yet current methods often overlook these dynamics in their mapping and planning strategies. To address this limitation, we present a framework that learns the evolving patterns of sea currents while simultaneously building a map of the seafloor. By integrating a sparse Gaussian process to model these changes over time, our approach effectively captures the dynamics without being overwhelmed by noise. The results of extensive simulations and real-world experiments reveal improved performance in predicting currents, reducing navigation errors, and generating more optimal trajectories. Temporal knowledge graphs are increasingly being utilized to derive practical inferences and forecast future relationships among entities. A new task, link forecasting, aims to predict future associations between entities that have been linked in the graph. Current approaches for link forecasting are divided into two categories: traditional machine learning methods and framework-based methods, with the latter offering more efficient performance but limited design of new schemes. To address this, we introduce static framework methods for link forecasting, allowing for the design of new schemes while maintaining efficiency. We evaluate three static framework approaches for link forecasting: homogeneous, inhomogeneous, and hypergraph-based framework models. Experimental results on two large-scale knowledge graphs reveal that these frameworks significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods, with the hypergraph model yielding the top performance in link forecasting. Additionally, we introduce a new metric to evaluate the generality of link forecasting models and demonstrate their practical value through successful predictions of future associations. These predicted links also facilitate the analysis of graph evolution and the detection of errors in the knowledge graph. Code and data are available for reproduction of our findings.

UGC 8839 is an extremely faint spiral galaxy that belongs to the Ursa Major cluster. Despite its low brightness, UGC 8839 has an unusually stable central disc, characterized by a constant rotation rate. Our research reveals that the central disc of UGC 8839 is not rotating at all, but rather is composed of a large, diffuse bar that spans approximately 10-15 kpc in diameter. This bar shape is supported by data from multiple sources, including our own, as well as a 1991 study by Hubble Space Telescope. Social media platforms like Twitter have become significant channels for disseminating and exchanging information about COVID-19. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are the leading models for 2D image classification, relying on a specific orientation of the convolution kernel. In this research, we introduce Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCNs) to enable flexible CNNs, allowing the convolution kernel to adapt its orientation during computation. We achieve this by incorporating a novel, efficient occlusion strategy for the activation function and a specific reformulation of the convolution operation. A crucial aspect of OCNs involves controlling the orientation of the convolution kernel, which we address by developing a novel, efficient method based on Grouped Orientational Filters (GOFs). Our experiments demonstrate that OCNs can be reduced to standard CNNs, specifically Deep Residual Networks (ResNets), by integrating GOFs with the occlusion strategy. As a result, OCNs offer a more compact and parameter-efficient alternative to CNNs. Our comprehensive evaluation on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets showcases the effectiveness of OCNs in reducing the number of parameters and depth, while achieving comparable or improved accuracy compared to CNNs. A significant parameter reduction of up to 50% is achieved by OCNs, along with a reduction of up to 20% in the number of layers. Furthermore, OCNs exhibit improved robustness against adversarial attacks and the ability to perform accurate image classification using randomly oriented convolution kernels. The source code of OCNs is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1994/Orientation-Convolutive-Networks.

Our experiments demonstrate that current defense methods are ineffective against SHTA and a proposed framework, called CleanTrigger, can successfully eliminate backdoors. The conditions necessary to achieve this phenomenon are discussed. As federated learning gains popularity, developers are concerned about the potential privacy breaches and biased aggregation results. To address these issues, we present FLVoogd, a refined federated learning framework that balances user privacy and robustness. The framework comprises an enhanced aggregation method, the Vooga algorithm, which calculates the global mean and median values while maintaining data privacy. The Vooga algorithm was compared to existing aggregation methods in three datasets and outperformed them in accuracy and fairness. Additionally, the framework was applied to a real-world language model, demonstrating improved performance and privacy compatibility. The source code for FLVoogd is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdelhakimBenboubker/FLVoogd.

This document outlines the approach of our team, "NoSignalNoDance", to the Sim2Real challenge. We utilized Deep Reinforcement Learning to train an autonomous agent in a simulated environment, which can navigate to a target point while avoiding obstacles. To bridge the gap between synthetic and real worlds, we developed a novel method of transferring policies by converting RGB images into grayscale for comparison. Our agent successfully completed the Sim2Real challenge, achieving 93% of the time in the final evaluation. A video demonstration of our results is available at https://youtu.be/6Q6Q8k6Q4g.

Unreal deepfakes are becoming increasingly prevalent, and their dissemination is accelerating the spread of misinformation. As deepfake technology improves, creating high-quality deepfakess becomes more accessible, even without sophisticated technical expertise. This ease of creation, combined with the rapid advancement of deepfake detection methods, makes real-world deepfake identification more feasible. Our research aims to address deepfake detection on unconstrained media in a robust manner. We introduce a novel deepfake dataset, called Deep-2-Face, which comprises high-resolution videos featuring two humans. This dataset serves as a testing ground for deepfake detection algorithms. Our analysis reveals that current methods struggle with Deep-2-Face deepfakes, and we introduce an enhanced strategy called CapsD, which significantly outperforms existing approaches on this dataset. CapsD's robust performance stems from its ability to detect deepfake lips and facial features, even when the nose and ear regions are manipulated. CapsD's effectiveness is further validated on the AFHQ dataset, where it surpasses state-of-the-art deepfake detection models. Our source code and Deep-2-Face dataset are available for public access.

Inspired by the human brain's efficiency and adaptability, spiking neural networks have the potential to revolutionize sequence processing tasks. However, current models relying on backpropagation through time face significant challenges due to the non-differentiable nature of spikes. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel, bio-plausible algorithm for learning spiking neural networks in a supervised manner. Our approach leverages the inherent properties of spikes to create a differentiable network, capable of processing temporal sequences. We have successfully applied this model to learning various temporal patterns, achieving remarkable accuracy and efficiency. Notably, our model has surpassed state-of-the-art results in multiple challenging time-series prediction tasks. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of a completely bio-plausible learning algorithm for spiking neural networks, enabling them to excel in sequence learning tasks. This report summarizes the findings of the Out-of-Context challenge, which was a key component of the 5th Multimodal Machine Learning for Human Body Shape Change workshop, held in conjunction with the 2021 International Conference on Computer Vision. The Out-of-Context challenge focused on detecting and mapping body parts in arbitrary images, given a person-specific reference image with clearly defined body parts. The challenge featured a novel, two-stage approach to processing the reference image and applying the resulting map to the input query. The detection phase utilized a Siamese network to identify the query image containing a person matching the reference, and the mapping phase applied an affine transformation to the detected person's map. The top-performing team achieved a score of 0.3236, significantly outperforming the second-best team. The report includes a detailed evaluation of the teams' performance and the results of the winning submission's optimization. This work introduces a method to evaluate the accuracy of generalized polynomial chaos expansions (GPC) outside of the initial approximation stage. Our approach generates a confidence interval for the partial sum of the expansions using classical error estimates and Navier-Stokes solution convergence criteria. This method is demonstrated by verifying a GPC representation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a finite domain with initial condition error and external data perturbation factors. The associated error analysis relies on the smoothness properties of the solutions to these equations, which are known to be $W^{2,\infty}$. The results of this study confirm the effectiveness of our proposed method in assessing the accuracy of the GPC representations. The corresponding numerical implementation is detailed, along with a comprehensive set of test cases that demonstrate the method's utility. The associated computer code can be accessed at \href{https://github.com/CMCS-EPFL/GPC-Verification}{github.com/CMCS-EPFL/GPC-Verification}. The authors believe that this work will contribute positively to the ongoing development of the GPC framework. The study identified potential areas for further improvement, such as the integration of a posteriori error control into the GPC approximation algorithm, and the exploration of alternative verification strategies that take advantage of the specific characteristics of the Navier-Stokes equations. The researchers also noted the importance of extending the developed methods to more complex scenarios, such as free boundary problems and three-dimensional domains. The study's conclusions and future research directions are summarized in Section 6. The authors also provided a detailed comparison of the used numerical methods in Appendix A. In various applications, sequential data changes occur, affecting either the mean or variance, which can be detected using Change-Point Analysis. However, this study expands on this concept by identifying and isolating periods of non-stationarity in partially-observed data streams. We introduce the concept of Partially-Observed Change-Point Analysis and propose the POCA problem, which involves identifying the start and end times of non-stationary periods, characterized by consistent sub-modes, in the presence of missing values. We present an Adaptive Partially-Observed Change-Point Detection (APOCPD) algorithm, which leverages the Gromov-Wasserstein graph matching to discover sub-modes and the Viterbi algorithm to track change periods, along with an efficient approximation, APPOCD. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in POCA scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashishgupta26/POCPD. Additionally, the results of our experiments can be found at https://ashishgupta26.github.io/POCPD. We will present our work in oral at NeurIPS 2021.
